en: The Treatise on the Essential Meaning of the Compendium of the Mother of Buddhas’ Prajñāpāramitā,
composed by the Bodhisattva Kṛṣṇapāda (Dpal dbyangs).
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao Feng Da Fu, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.

Translated by the Imperial Preceptor for the Transmission of the Dharma, the Purple-Robed Subject Shi Hu, and others, by imperial decree: I take refuge in the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta and the rest.
The accomplishment of Prajñāpāramitā and so forth, The Tathāgata of Non-dual Wisdom, And the correspondence with the meaning therein— These are the two paths of its vocal teaching.
The basis and the function, the undertaking of the activity and its cultivation,
the conceptual characteristics and the transgressions, and the praise— these are explained in their respective order.
Having faith as its essence, it is taught through the mutual testimony of teacher and disciple.
Regarding the time and place of the teaching and so forth, one attains the accomplishment of personal authority (*pramāṇa*).
The speaker of the Dharma should know that when both the time and place in the world are corroborated by witnesses for the speaker,
only then does one attain the authority of the teaching (*yathārtha-pramāṇa*).
All such collections, as taught by me and others, harmonize with this meaning;
these thirty-two supreme [aspects] are analyzed into sixteen characteristics, and emptiness follows their respective order.
It is taught in the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, understood as being taught through various skillful means.
This present *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* does not diminish the meaning as it was taught;
though the verses have been abbreviated according to preference, the meaning remains exactly as it was taught.
I do not perceive a "Bodhisattva"; this teaching is truly silent.
That which can receive internal phenomena is said to be emptiness.
Form and the intrinsic nature of form—this teaching is likewise empty.
In these external sense bases, all perceived portions cease.
Regarding the characteristics of that body— such as form— and its abiding or its separation,
if one views them according to their true meaning, they are found to be without reality within.
Those various internal emptinesses are themselves empty of intrinsic nature;
regarding all seeds of the characteristics of consciousness, I give rise to compassion and wisdom.
Neither arising nor ceasing—sentient beings are thus clarified.
The desire for the birth and death of sentient beings is said by him to be emptiness.
The Buddha-dharma is unperceivable, and the Bodhisattva-dharma is likewise;
as it has been taught, these, including the ten powers and so forth, are empty.
The various individual phenomena are said to be the nature of pervasive conceptualization (parikalpita-svabhāva);
they do not exist in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), and all phenomena are explained in this way.
The Great Being (mahāsattva) ultimately effects the severance of those views of self and so forth.
That person has no self; the Buddha has taught this in all places.
All phenomena are unarisen; this which is taught is likewise so.
He proclaims the selflessness of phenomena; he speaks the truth in all places.
Faults and their absences neither increase nor decrease;
all conditioned and unconditioned things, as well as every form of virtue, come to rest within emptiness.
From within that emptiness, those virtues emerge again, inexhaustible.
This pervasive conceptual construction is universally subsumed as emptiness.
Through the ten types of mental distraction—mental distraction toward other objects—the deluded fail to attain correspondence; thus, non-dual wisdom is not realized.
Their mutual cessation serves as the remedy for the subject and the object;
this is what is fully set forth in the teaching of Prajñāpāramitā.
If a bodhisattva possesses this non-conceptualization of signs, [he attains liberation].
The Teacher who has stilled all distraction Expounded those conventional aggregates.
In these Eight Thousand Verses and others, From the sequence of the opening words until their conclusion,
He taught the cessation of all things, Explaining the non-existence of conceptual construction.
Because it is not as stated, this merely explains conventional phenomena;
in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and other scriptures, one knows all things according to reality.
I do not perceive a "bodhisattva" apart from these vast [phenomena].
World-Honored One, this cessation dispels the confusion of conceptualization regarding signs.
If one does not perceive those names, the same applies to the activity within the objective sphere;
in all those aggregates and locations, the Bodhisattva is nowhere to be seen.
This negates pervasive conceptual construction and universally encompasses all that has been taught;
it is the vehicle of the cause for omniscience, wherein wisdom discerns all characteristics.
The Prajñāpāramitā explains three types of reliance.
That is to say: the thoroughly imagined, the dependent, and the perfected nature.
When these conceptual phrases are absent, all pervasive imagining ceases;
through the vision of similes such as illusions, this explains the dependent nature.
There are four kinds of purity; The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is thus explained.
The Prajñāpāramitā— The Buddha has no other teaching than this.
Regarding the ten types of conceptual distraction, Their remedies are taught in corresponding order.
Having understood these three types [of knowledge], they are explained as being either identical or distinct.
Just as the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) was first discussed, so too are the dependent (*paratantra*) and the imagined (*parikalpita*).
By means of the signless (*animitta*) and the analytical discernment of form (*rūpa*), those distractions are stilled and dispelled.
That Buddha is also awakening; one does not perceive a speaker or anything equal [to it].
Upon reaching the final completion of this knowledge, the imputed nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) is ceased and dispelled.
Since that form is empty of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-śūnya), what could possibly exist as its characteristic (lakṣaṇa)?
Within these distinct expressions, having understood them, one brings them to rest.
Because this is not empty, it is empty; such is what is taught by these words.
All conceptualizations of denigration and all such discourses are thereby brought to cessation.
The Buddha is likewise like an illusion, and he is likewise like a dream;
knowing this according to the sequence, the limit of the Sage’s speech is certain.
All that is performed by those who are equal [to him] is here described as the Buddha being like an illusion.
The words "like an illusion" and so forth describe the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Since the wisdom of ordinary beings is pure by its very nature, it is said that they are Buddhas; thus, Bodhisattvas are also like Buddhas.
The self-nature is obscured by its own form; that which is produced by the cause of ignorance appears as various distinctions like a magical illusion. The fruit is like a dream and is abandoned;
though non-dual, it is spoken of as distinct, and thus the fruit and so forth are certainly subject to deprecation.
Those who slander all conceptual constructions are slandering this teaching.
Form and emptiness are not a composite; they would be mutually contradictory [if so].
Where there is no form, there is no name of "emptiness"; it is the characteristics of form itself that are naturally in harmony.
This single nature-discrimination serves as the antidote to various natures;
emptiness is not different from that form—what, then, exists within that emptiness?
This is what appears without reality; it arises from ignorance.
This lack of reality is what expresses it, for that is called ignorance.
This is how form is described: the perfection of wisdom is non-dual;
such duality is the antidote to dualistic discrimination.
The purity of the nature as spoken of according to reality is likewise unattainable;
through the contradiction between existence and non-existence, various natures are definitively perceived.
It is taught that this form is a mere name, for in truth it lacks intrinsic nature.
That conceptualization of intrinsic nature should cease as soon as it arises.
Form and the intrinsic nature of form are empty, just as previously explained;
that conceptualization which [clings] to both the intrinsic nature and its characteristics is here refuted.
Regarding all phenomena such as non-arising and non-ceasing,
the Buddha taught that if one views them as scattered or distinct, those are merely conceptual distinctions.
Such things as false designations and conventional names— if one discriminates those phenomena [in that way], [they are but mental constructs].
Sound and meaning are not conjoined; they are not of the nature of selfhood.
So it is with the Prajñāpāramitā and likewise with the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas:
these are merely names spoken, devoid of any conceptualization of real entities.
When all meanings of sounds cease, this is not the cessation of things themselves;
know that it is likewise with the rest, for the meaning within speech is determined.
This non-apprehension is correct; thus one truly knows all names and realities.
As the nature of meaning is thus, it does not cease by means of excluding that sound.
Subhūti is doubly detached; such is the meaning of sound within sound.
The Bodhisattva has no name; I see this and speak of its existence.
In the Prajñāpāramitā, speech does not arise with fixed determination;
its investigation belongs only to the wise, for this meaning is subtle wisdom.
The meaning of continuity is dispelled; if one discriminates it as having a separate meaning, [it is not so].
The Prajñāpāramitā—its verbal expression is like an echo.
Summarizing this meaning: it is the basis for [the term] "Prajñā" and so forth;
thus the meaning recurs, serving as the basis for further distinct meanings.
The Prajñāpāramitā, correctly condensed into eight thousand verses—
whatever mass of merit is obtained from that all arises from the Prajñā.
*The Treatise on the Essential Meaning of the Compendium of the Mother of Buddhas, the Prajñāpāramitā*.
